title: Open problem: improved quantitative rank bounds
statement_text: It would be very interesting to get better lower bounds on the rank of $n\times n$ complex matrices whose non-diagonal entries lie in a multiplicative group $G\subseteq\mathbb{C}^*$ of rank at most $r$ and whose diagonal entries do not lie in $G$, even for cases where the rank of the multiplicative group is very small, for example when all non-diagonal elements are powers of two (and the diagonal elements are not).
context_text: All matrices are $n\times n$ complex matrices, and the rank of a multiplicative subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb{C}^*$ is its rank as an abelian group (the maximum number of multiplicatively independent elements; e.g. the powers of 2 form a group of rank 1). The authors' main theorem says that for all positive integers $r$ and $D$ there is $n_0(r,D)$ such that if $G$ has rank at most $r$, $M=(m_{ij})$ is an $n\times n$ matrix with $n\ge n_0$, $m_{ij}\in G$ for all $i\ne j$ and $m_{jj}\notin G$ for all $j$, then $\mathrm{rank}(M)\ge D$. The proofs rely on the Subspace Theorem of Evertse, Schlickewei and Schmidt; the first gives roughly $\log\log n\le rd^7$ for a matrix of rank $d$, and the second improves this to $\log n\le rd^8$, i.e. $d\ge(\log n/r)^{1/8}$, which the authors still consider weak. Even the special case of determining the minimum possible rank of an $n\times n$ matrix whose non-diagonal elements are powers of 2 and whose diagonal elements are not is intriguing: the minimum tends to infinity with $n$, but the lower bound is probably far from tight, and a Gram-matrix construction from the affine planes of $\mathbb{F}_3^d$ plus an extra point shows that it is at most $O(n^{1/3})$. Applications include the fact that distance sets of finite point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$ generate multiplicative groups of high rank.
